newsitem.title: FINLAND: Soviet-US Cold War air battle over Finland - report.
newsitem.headline: Soviet-US Cold War air battle over Finland - report.

text.p: Finnish media have uncovered evidence of a Cold War air skirmish between U.S. and Soviet warplanes in the 1950s which Finland denied at the time to preserve the country's delicate neutrality.

A Finnish television report late on Monday said that in May 1954 Soviet MiG 15 fighters attacked three U.S. RB-47 bombers, which were on an unauthorised intelligence mission over the northern Kola Peninsula. The attack on one U.S. plane went into Finnish airspace.

The report emerged just days after Washington announced plans for U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin to hold their next summit in Helsinki, a key venue for diplomatic encounters between East and West during the Cold War.
The television showed witnesses and a leading veteran politician confirming the skirmish took place, and said documents released since also proved it happened.

The U.S. bombers eventually escaped, returning to base in Britain, but the incident could have heightened superpower tension. Six years later in 1960, Soviet forces shot down a U.S. U2 spy plane over Russia, causing a diplomatic storm.
The Finnish Foreign Ministry declined to comment on the television report.
"At first I thought it was thunder," recalled retired Warrant Officer Eero Laine, patrolling at the time near Finland's 1,300 km (800 mile) border with the then Soviet Union.
"Then I realised, damn, they are coming to our side...and when they were well on our side, we heard ta-ta-ta-ta, ta-ta-ta-ta, and realised it could not be a breach of the sound barrier."
Retired U.S. Colonel Carl Holt , pilot of one of the American planes, said: "At one point I counted that about 10 MiG 15s were attacking us."
Holt's plane was hit and started losing fuel before the MiGs turned back. After refuelling above the Norwegian Sea he returned to base.

Acccording to the report, the U.S. mission was to photograph Soviet military establishments and potential targets for nuclear weapons, despite orders from President Dwight Eisenhower to refrain from such operations.
The mission was masterminded by the then strongly anti-Communist commander of U.S. strategic air forces, Curtis Le May, who has since died, the report said.
Finnish newspaper Uusi Suomi reported the incident in 1954, but officials dismissed it as humbug.
"We feared that we could easily have been misunderstood (as belonging to) one or the other side," said former prime minister Johannes Virolainen, a cabinet member at the time.
"It was (an event) that had to do with the relations between the two superpowers, the U.S. and the Soviet Union, and not directly to us," said Virolainen.
"We knew that such things happened all the time and of course they were all noted, handled and given notice of diplomatically, but we would not exaggerate them."

During World War Two, Finland survived two wars against the Soviet Union without occupation, and although it was officially neutral during the Cold War it had a cooperation treaty with the USSR which distanced it from Europe's post-war integration.

Since the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, Finland has leaned increasingly towards the West. Since joining the European Union in 1995, it has preferred to call its defence policy position independent rather than neutral.
